A BlitzLLVM extension: shows the window in HDR on a display that has HDR switched on (in Windows 11: Settings, System, Display, HDR). Without HDR a program is shown as it always was, and the system's own Auto HDR can only touch it where Windows decides to, which depends on the program. AutoHDR does it for the program itself: the picture is made linear, scaled so that SDR white has the brightness that the system has set for SDR content (the slider "SDR content brightness"; [AutoHDRWhite](AutoHDRWhite) overrides it), and sent to the window as scRGB (a 16 bit floating point swapchain), which the system shows without changing it. With mode 2 the bright parts of the picture are also stretched toward the peak of the display ([AutoHDRPeak](AutoHDRPeak), [AutoHDRExpand](AutoHDRExpand)), which is what makes the picture look like it does with the Auto HDR of Windows: mid tones stay where they were and only highlights are lifted. The Auto HDR of Windows works differently and its algorithm is not public, so this is a look-alike and not the same picture. It works in a window and fullscreen, needs the driver to offer scRGB for the window (see [HWHDRSupported](HWHDRSupported)), and does nothing where it is not offered: the window then keeps its normal swapchain, so asking for it is always safe. It can be called before [Graphics](Graphics) and changed at any time; the window changes at the next [Flip](Flip). [ReadPixel](ReadPixel), [SaveBuffer](SaveBuffer) and the like see the buffer, not the HDR picture, and nothing about the picture changes on a display without HDR. Mode 3 is for programs that draw in HDR on purpose, with a 64 bit buffer (a depth of 64 in [Graphics3D](Graphics3D), whose pixels are half floats that may be above 1) or a 30 bit one: the buffer is shown with all of its precision and nothing is lifted, 1.0 is SDR white, and values above 1 are brighter up to the peak of the display. An 8 bit buffer is shown as with mode 1, and a buffer with gamma tables or a palette is shown through the 8 bit picture of those. It is on by default (mode 2), and does nothing where the display or driver has no HDR. `AutoHDR 0` or the environment variable `BLITZLLVM_AUTOHDR=0` turns it off; `BLITZLLVM_AUTOHDR` sets the mode a program starts with.
@param mode  0 for no HDR, 1 for the same picture in HDR, 2 to also lift the highlights, 3 to show a buffer of more than 8 bits as it is. It is 2 by default, so a program is shown in HDR on a display that supports it without asking.
